boss.q: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. Demand falls while supply also falls. Why is the rate direction ambiguous?
options: Both shifts push it down by different amounts
Supply determines only the rate and demand only quantity
Supply prevents any exchange-rate change
Lower demand pushes it down, while lower supply pushes it up
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: The shifts exert opposing pressure on the vertical-axis price, so magnitudes decide the net change.

boss.q: Refer to the graph. By what percentage does the rate fall when supply increases?
options: 16.7 percent
12.5 percent
20 percent
25 percent
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: The rate falls 0.2 from an initial 1.0; 0.2 divided by 1.0 is 20 percent.
boss.imageAlt: Upward-sloping dollar supply shifts right from S0 to S1 along demand D0.
boss.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand D0 is unchanged while supply shifts right from solid S0 to dashed S1. Equilibrium moves from A at quantity 100 and rate 1.0 to B at quantity 150 and rate 0.8.
boss.foreignExchangeScenario: Increase in supply of U.S. dollars

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the conceptual graph with upward-sloping supply. Foreign export demand shifts D0 to D1 and residents’ foreign-asset purchases shift S0 to S1. Separately, foreign purchases of domestic assets are known to be unchanged. Which conclusion distinguishes graph evidence from asset accounting?
options: The unchanged rate alone proves unchanged NCO even though residents buy more foreign assets
The gross dollar quantity alone equals NCO in every upward-sloping currency market
The displayed quantity rises and the rate rises; the identity permits NX to fall despite higher NCO
The displayed dollar quantity rises and the rate is unchanged; the separate net-asset evidence establishes higher NCO and therefore NX
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph provides a rightward final intersection at the same vertical level. NCO rises because resident foreign purchases rise with the inward asset flow fixed, not because gross currency turnover is itself NCO. In consistent accounts, NX matches that higher NCO.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market showing demand and upward-sloping supply both shifting right.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand shifts right from D0 to D1 and supply shifts right from S0 to S1. The displayed shifts raise equilibrium quantity while leaving the exchange rate at the same vertical position. No numerical ticks are shown.
legendaryBoss.foreignExchangeScenario: Conceptual simultaneous increases in demand and supply

legendaryBoss.q: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. At the original exchange rate, an export-demand shock increases dollars demanded by 70 units and an asset-purchase shock increases dollars supplied by 45 units. What happens to equilibrium e and quantity, and do those two shift amounts identify their exact changes?
options: Both rise; e rises exactly 25 percent
e falls and quantity rises; supply determines the rate independently
Both rise; curve slopes are needed for exact changes
e is unchanged and quantity rises exactly 115 units
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendaryBoss.feedback: At the old rate, excess demand is 70 − 45 = 25 units, so e rises. Both rightward shifts increase equilibrium quantity. Horizontal shift amounts at a common rate sign the change but do not determine exact rate or quantity changes without slopes.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the numbered graph. Compare demand-first and supply-first adjustment, assuming each market clears before the second shift and final curves are identical. Which statement distinguishes the paths from the endpoint?
options: Both paths temporarily raise the rate because final quantity is larger
Demand first temporarily raises the rate and supply first temporarily lowers it; both end at B
Demand first ends at a permanently higher rate than supply first
Both paths have a constant rate because A and B have the same rate
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendaryBoss.feedback: D1 with S0 crosses above A; D0 with S1 crosses below A. Once both changes occur, each path ends at the same unique D1-S1 intersection B. An unchanged endpoint does not imply an unchanged intermediate rate.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Dollar demand and upward-sloping supply both shift right, from D0 and S0 to D1 and S1.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand and supply both shift right. Original equilibrium A is quantity 100 and rate 1.0; final equilibrium B is quantity 200 and rate 1.0. Solid curves are D0 and S0; dashed curves are D1 and S1. D1 crosses S0 at approximately quantity 150 and rate 1.2; D0 crosses S1 at approximately quantity 150 and rate 0.8. These two crossings have no point labels or dashed coordinate guides.
legendaryBoss.foreignExchangeScenario: Simultaneous increases in demand and supply

repairQuestions.q: In the NCO-based FX model, NCO is fixed. A student says a higher exchange rate must increase the quantity supplied. Which correction distinguishes a movement along vertical supply from a shift?
options: Moving up the vertical supply curve raises both NCO and supplied quantity
A higher exchange rate shifts vertical supply right even with NCO fixed
Moving along vertical supply requires an increase in foreign demand at every rate
Moving up the vertical supply curve leaves quantity fixed; changing NCO shifts that curve
repairQuestions.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
repairQuestions.feedback: A vertical supply curve contains multiple exchange rates at one quantity. Moving along it does not change NCO; a change in NCO moves the whole curve horizontally. A separate demand shift can produce a new equilibrium rate at the same supplied quantity.

bridgeQuestions.q: A real depreciation occurs in the currency market. How does that change connect to aggregate demand?
options: The depreciation shifts short-run aggregate supply left
Higher net exports shift aggregate demand right
Lower net exports shift aggregate demand left
Domestic investment becomes zero
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Real depreciation makes domestic goods relatively cheaper, tending to raise NX; because NX is an AD component, aggregate demand increases.

open-economy-policy-transmission.title: Open-Economy Policy and Macroeconomic Transmission
open-economy-policy-transmission.description: Trace fiscal policy, trade policy, capital flight, and monetary changes through saving, interest rates, NCO, exchange rates, net exports, and aggregate demand.

easy.q: In the standard open-economy model, a larger government budget deficit first reduces:
options: Foreign saving
Net exports by accounting definition
The domestic price level
National saving
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A larger deficit lowers public saving and therefore national saving when private saving is unchanged.

easy.q: A decline in national saving shifts the supply of loanable funds:
options: Vertically upward without changing quantity
Into the foreign-exchange demand curve
Left
Right
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: National saving supplies loanable funds, so less saving shifts that supply left.

easy.q: When the domestic real interest rate rises, net capital outflow tends to:
options: Equal government purchases
Fall
Rise
Remain fixed
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Higher domestic returns make domestic assets more attractive, reducing NCO.

easy.q: A fall in NCO shifts the supply of domestic currency in foreign exchange:
options: Left
Right
Down along the same vertical curve
Into currency demand
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Fewer net foreign-asset purchases mean less domestic currency is supplied for exchange.

easy.q: A real appreciation tends to change net exports in which direction?
options: Up
Toward domestic investment
Not at all
Down
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Appreciation makes domestic goods relatively expensive and foreign goods relatively cheap, reducing NX.

easy.q: Capital flight begins with an increase in desired:
options: Foreign purchases of domestic goods
Domestic tax revenue
Foreign-asset purchases
Domestic consumption only
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Political or economic risk can prompt residents and investors to move portfolios toward foreign assets.

medium.q: Which chain correctly begins the textbook effect of a larger budget deficit?
options: National saving rises, so the real interest rate falls
Investment demand falls, so NCO rises
Currency demand rises, so public saving rises
National saving falls, so the real interest rate rises
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Lower public saving reduces loanable-funds supply and raises the equilibrium real rate.

medium.q: A higher domestic real interest rate caused by a deficit changes the foreign-exchange market by:
options: Reducing exports and shifting currency demand left first
Increasing saving and shifting currency demand right
Reducing NCO and shifting currency supply left
Increasing NCO and shifting currency supply right
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The higher return attracts funds toward domestic assets, so fewer domestic-currency units are supplied to acquire foreign assets.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What happens to the U.S. dollar when NCO-determined supply shifts left from S0 to S1?
options: It appreciates while the dollar quantity rises from 50 to 100
It appreciates from 1.0 to 1.5 foreign-currency units per dollar
It depreciates from 1.5 to 1.0 foreign-currency units per dollar
It remains fixed because NX equals NCO
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The leftward supply shift moves equilibrium from A to B, raising the foreign-currency price of a dollar while reducing quantity from 100 to 50.
medium.imageAlt: Mankiw-model dollar market with vertical supply shifting left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1 along D0 equals NX0.
medium.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 equals NX0. Vertical supply shifts left from S0 equals NCO0 at quantity 100 to S1 equals NCO1 at quantity 50. Equilibrium moves from A at rate 1.0 to B at rate 1.5.
medium.foreignExchangeScenario: Decrease in NCO-determined supply of U.S. dollars

medium.q: Why does a real currency appreciation tend to reduce aggregate demand, holding its other components fixed?
options: It lowers net exports, a component of aggregate demand
It lowers the domestic money supply by identity
It raises government purchases
It shifts long-run aggregate supply left
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Relatively expensive domestic goods reduce exports and encourage imports, lowering NX and AD.

medium.q: An import quota directly reduces import demand. In the standard long-run open-economy model with NCO fixed, what offsets this effect?
options: A fall in national saving that raises NCO
A currency depreciation that raises exports further
A fall in domestic investment equal to the quota
A real appreciation that reduces exports and encourages other imports
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The quota raises demand for domestic currency, but appreciation brings NX back to the level fixed by NCO.

medium.q: Political instability triggers capital flight. What happens to currency supply in foreign exchange?
options: Currency demand shifts right
It stays fixed because capital flows use asset markets
It shifts right
It shifts left
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Higher NCO means more domestic currency is offered to purchase foreign assets.

hard.q: Which complete chain follows a larger budget deficit in the standard model?
options: Saving falls → real interest rate rises → NCO falls → currency appreciates → NX falls
Saving falls → real interest rate falls → NCO rises → currency appreciates → NX rises
Saving rises → real interest rate rises → NCO rises → currency depreciates → NX falls
Saving falls → NCO rises → currency supply falls → currency depreciates → NX rises
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The deficit lowers public and national saving, raising the real rate; lower NCO reduces FX supply, producing appreciation and lower net exports.

hard.q: A tariff is imposed while national saving and domestic investment remain unchanged. What is the general-equilibrium NX result in the textbook model?
options: NX rises because lower imports change the trade balance while NCO stays fixed
NX falls because appreciation reduces exports by more than the tariff changes imports
NX becomes positive because the tariff shifts currency demand right
NX is unchanged after currency appreciation offsets the direct import reduction
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Unchanged S and I fix NCO = S − I and hence NX. The tariff raises demand for domestic currency, causing real exchange-rate appreciation until exports and other imports adjust enough to preserve that NX balance. This is an exchange-rate change, not a claim that the real interest rate rises.

hard.q: Political risk raises desired NCO. Why does this shift demand for loanable funds right and tend to raise the real interest rate?
options: The foreign-exchange rate becomes the price in the loanable-funds market
Government purchases replace domestic investment in the saving identity
National saving must finance both domestic investment and the larger NCO
Household consumption becomes part of NCO when political risk rises
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: National saving finances I + NCO, so a larger desired NCO raises total demand for loanable funds at each real interest rate.

hard.q: Political risk raises desired NCO and the equilibrium real interest rate. Which two-market outcome follows?
options: Domestic investment rises while the currency depreciates
Domestic investment falls while the domestic currency depreciates
Domestic investment rises while the currency appreciates
Domestic investment falls while the currency appreciates
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The higher loanable-funds rate crowds out domestic investment, while greater NCO shifts currency supply right and lowers the exchange rate.

hard.q: Expansionary monetary policy lowers the domestic real interest rate in the short run. Hold domestic and foreign goods prices and other asset-return determinants fixed. Which open-economy channel reinforces aggregate demand?
options: NCO rises, the currency depreciates, and NX rises
NCO falls, the currency appreciates, and NX falls
NCO rises, the currency appreciates, and NX falls
NCO falls, the currency depreciates, and NX falls
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Lower domestic returns increase NCO, which raises currency supply, causes depreciation, and supports net exports.

hard.q: A government deficit rises while foreign interest rates also rise. What is the direction of domestic NCO?
options: It falls because the domestic fiscal change receives greater weight
It rises because foreign rates determine the relevant return by themselves
It is unchanged because the NX identity offsets both rate changes
Ambiguous because the domestic-rate and foreign-rate channels oppose each other
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The deficit-driven domestic rate rise tends to reduce NCO, while higher foreign returns tend to increase it.

elite.q: A tariff reduces imports directly while a simultaneous budget deficit reduces national saving. What can be said about net exports?
options: Both policies raise NX through lower imports and lower saving
The tariff raises NX while the deficit changes only domestic investment
Tariff appreciation and deficit depreciation offset, leaving NX unchanged
Tariff effects are offset in equilibrium; the deficit tends to lower NX
elite.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
elite.feedback: Trade policy is offset by appreciation when NCO is fixed; the deficit lowers NCO and therefore lowers the equilibrium NX balance.

elite.q: In a short-run comparison before full trade and output adjustment, monetary easing lowers domestic real rates while a foreign recession cuts export demand. Prices are fixed, and NCO is not held fixed across the two shocks. Can the net AD change be signed without response magnitudes?
options: AD falls because foreign income changes exports while monetary policy changes only investment
AD is unchanged because depreciation offsets the export-demand shift one for one
Ambiguous without the relative strengths of higher NX from depreciation and lower export demand
AD rises because the monetary channel determines the exchange rate before exports respond
elite.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
elite.feedback: Easing supports domestic investment and, through depreciation, NX. Foreign recession reduces demand for exports. Their short-run AD contributions compete. The fixed-NCO long-run trade-offset result cannot be imposed on this adjustment comparison.

legendary.q: A larger deficit raises the domestic real interest rate, but an even larger rise in foreign rates occurs. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: NCO may rise despite the deficit, so the exchange-rate and NX effects are not determined from the deficit alone
NCO falls because the budget deficit initiates the domestic saving channel
The currency appreciates because increases in both rates favor domestic assets
NX falls by the deficit change because fiscal and trade balances move together
legendary.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendary.feedback: Capital flows respond to relative returns. The foreign-rate shock can dominate the usual deficit-induced decline in NCO.

legendary.q: In the open-economy loanable-funds model, saving is unchanged and capital flight raises desired NCO $150 billion at the original real interest rate. Final domestic investment falls $110 billion. Reconstruct the rate-induced NCO feedback and FX outcome with NX demand and price levels fixed.
options: Feedback raises NCO $40 billion; final NCO rises $190 billion and the currency depreciates
Feedback lowers NCO $110 billion; final NCO rises $40 billion and the currency appreciates
Feedback exactly cancels the shock; NCO and the exchange rate are unchanged
Feedback lowers NCO $40 billion; final NCO rises $110 billion and the currency depreciates
legendary.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendary.feedback: With ΔS=0 and ΔI=−110, ΔNCO=110. Relative to the initial +150 schedule shift, rate feedback is −40. Final vertical FX supply shifts right by 110, lowering the foreign-currency-per-domestic-currency rate and raising NX.

legendary.q: A trade restriction initially lowers targeted imports by $64 billion. After exchange-rate adjustment, exports are $37 billion lower. Saving and investment are unchanged. What rebound in other imports reconciles the accounts, and what would a measured rebound of only $20 billion imply if all figures were complete and exact?
options: A $101 billion rebound is required; a $20 billion rebound confirms unchanged NX
A $27 billion rebound is required; a $20 billion rebound would still leave NX unchanged
A $27 billion rebound is required; a $20 billion rebound would conflict with unchanged S and I
A $37 billion rebound is required; a $20 billion rebound proves a larger NCO
legendary.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendary.feedback: Unchanged S−I requires ΔNX=0. Solve 0=−37−(−64+rebound), so rebound=27. If it were only 20, ΔNX=7, contradicting the stipulated unchanged saving-investment balance; at least one assumption or measurement must differ.

legendary.q: Monetary tightening raises the domestic interest rate, while political risk simultaneously rises. What can be concluded about the currency?
options: It is unchanged because monetary policy affects the nominal rate while risk affects the real rate
Its direction is ambiguous because lower NCO from returns opposes higher NCO from risk
It appreciates because the policy-rate channel is transmitted before portfolios rebalance
It depreciates because political risk shifts currency demand rather than supply
legendary.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendary.feedback: Higher returns tend to reduce currency supply and appreciate the currency; higher risk tends to raise supply and depreciate it.

legendary.q: A budget deficit reduces NCO by $60 billion. A simultaneous rise in foreign demand shifts currency demand right enough to raise the exchange rate further. What happens to NX?
options: It falls $60 billion even though both FX shifts appreciate the currency
It rises because foreign demand dominates
It is unchanged because appreciation offsets the deficit
It falls by the unknown demand shift rather than by NCO
legendary.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendary.feedback: The accounting identity fixes NX at the new NCO, down $60 billion; stronger foreign demand changes the exchange rate needed to reach that balance.

legendary.q: After capital flight, the real interest rate rises and domestic investment falls. Why can NCO still be higher?
options: The higher interest rate moves NCO outward along its unchanged relationship
Domestic investment and NCO move together because both use national saving
Capital flight reclassifies foreign assets as domestic investment
The outward shift in desired foreign assets exceeds the rate-induced movement back toward domestic assets
legendary.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendary.feedback: The risk shock shifts the NCO relationship outward; the higher rate partly offsets but need not reverse that shift.

boss.q: A government deficit reduces public saving. If private saving is unchanged, national saving:
options: Becomes equal to taxes
Falls
Rises
Stays fixed
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: National saving is private plus public saving, so a lower public component reduces the total.

boss.q: With dollar demand unchanged and the vertical axis quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar, a leftward dollar-supply shift causes the dollar to:
options: Appreciate
Depreciate
Remain fixed
Lose all foreign purchasing power
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: With currency demand unchanged, reduced supply raises the equilibrium exchange rate.

boss.q: Which event most directly initiates capital flight?
options: A fall in foreign demand for domestic exports
A balanced government budget
A decline in domestic import prices
A sharp rise in perceived domestic political risk
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: Greater perceived risk prompts investors to move assets abroad.

boss.q: Refer to the conceptual graph. A deficit raises domestic rates and lowers NCO. Which displayed change represents the next link?
options: Vertical dollar supply shifts left from S0 to S1
Dollar demand shifts right from D0 to D1
Vertical dollar supply shifts right from S1 to S0
Dollar demand becomes vertical at S0
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: Lower NCO means fewer dollars are exchanged for foreign assets, represented by the leftward shift in NCO-determined supply.
boss.imageAlt: Conceptual Mankiw-model dollar market with vertical supply shifting left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1.
boss.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 equals NX0. Vertical supply shifts left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1, so the new intersection is above and left of the original intersection. No numerical ticks or point labels are shown.
boss.foreignExchangeScenario: Conceptual decrease in NCO-determined supply of U.S. dollars

boss.q: Why does an import quota fail to guarantee higher NX in the textbook model?
options: Quotas increase national saving by the import reduction
Foreigners stop demanding domestic currency
The quota raises domestic investment by identity
Exchange-rate appreciation offsets the direct trade effect when NCO is fixed
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: Trade policy changes currency demand and the real exchange rate, but not the saving-investment balance that sets NCO and NX.

boss.q: In a short-run dollar market with upward-sloping supply, fixed domestic and foreign prices, and e quoted in foreign currency per dollar, a foreign recession reduces export demand. Which immediate demand and exchange-rate channel follows?
options: Loanable-funds supply rises and appreciation cushions the export-demand loss
Dollar demand rises and depreciation reinforces the export-demand loss
Dollar demand falls and depreciation cushions the initial export-demand loss
Dollar supply falls and appreciation raises net exports
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: Weaker foreign demand shifts dollar demand left. With upward-sloping supply, e falls; fixed prices make this a real depreciation that cushions the initial goods-demand loss. This conditional short-run channel does not assert a permanent NX decline in the separate fixed-NCO model.

boss.q: The government deficit widens and private saving rises by the same amount. What happens through the national-saving channel?
options: National saving falls by twice the deficit change, strengthening the usual chain
NCO falls because public saving receives more weight than private saving
The currency appreciates because the deficit shifts FX supply directly
National saving is unchanged, so the standard deficit chain need not begin
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: The offsetting private-saving increase leaves total national saving unchanged, removing the stated first link.

boss.q: Capital flight raises NCO and the real interest rate. Which outcomes follow in the two markets?
options: More currency demand, appreciation, and less investment
Less currency demand, depreciation, and more investment
More currency supply, depreciation, and less domestic investment
Less currency supply, appreciation, and more investment
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: Higher NCO shifts FX supply right, while the higher loanable-funds rate crowds out some domestic investment.

boss.q: In a short-run comparison with goods prices fixed, monetary easing lowers domestic real returns while stronger foreign income increases demand for domestic exports. Which FX channels initially support domestic aggregate demand?
options: Both changes lower currency demand
Easing raises currency supply; stronger foreign income raises currency demand
Both changes reduce currency supply
Easing raises currency demand; foreign income raises currency supply
boss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
boss.feedback: Lower domestic rates raise NCO and currency supply, while higher foreign purchases of exports raise currency demand.

legendaryBoss.q: A fiscal change reduces public saving by $80 billion. Private saving rises by an unknown amount. Real interest rates rise, domestic investment falls $30 billion, and NX falls $35 billion. What private-saving response reconciles the model, and how does FX supply move?
options: Private saving rises $45 billion; vertical FX supply falls $80 billion
Private saving falls $15 billion; vertical FX supply rises $35 billion
Private saving rises $15 billion; vertical FX supply falls $35 billion
Private saving rises $115 billion; vertical FX supply is unchanged
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Let p be the private-saving rise. ΔNX=ΔNCO=(p−80)−(−30)=p−50=−35, so p=15. Net saving falls 65 and investment falls 30, leaving NCO and vertical FX supply down 35.

legendaryBoss.q: In the vertical-NCO FX model, a tariff and capital flight occur together. At the original exchange rate, the tariff raises currency demand by 40 units while the final NCO increase raises supply by 65 units after interest-rate feedback. Prices and other demand determinants are fixed. What follows, and which extra information would quantify the exchange-rate change?
options: The currency appreciates and NX rises 40 units; the loanable-funds supply slope alone measures appreciation
The currency depreciates and NX rises 65 units; the NX-demand slope is needed to quantify depreciation
The currency depreciates but NX is unchanged; tariffs fix the trade balance
The rate is unchanged and NX rises 105 units; horizontal shifts can simply be added
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendaryBoss.feedback: At the old rate, supply rises 25 units more than demand, creating excess supply. The foreign-currency-per-domestic-currency quote falls until demand matches final NCO. NX rises 65 by identity; the remaining exchange-rate change requires the NX-demand response.

legendaryBoss.q: Monetary easing lowers rates and raises NCO by $45 billion. A simultaneous export-demand shock raises currency demand but does not change saving or investment. What happens to NX?
options: It rises $45 billion; the demand shock affects the exchange rate needed to achieve that balance
It rises by an unknown amount because demand sets NX independently
It is unchanged because the two FX shifts offset
It falls $45 billion because currency supply rises
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
legendaryBoss.feedback: NX equals NCO, so the balance rises $45 billion. The separate demand shift changes the equilibrium rate, not the accounting equality.

repairQuestions.q: A student says a budget deficit raises NCO because government borrowing sends funds abroad. Which link corrects the chain?
options: Government borrowing shifts currency demand right directly
NCO rises whenever public saving falls
The higher domestic real interest rate reduces NCO
The deficit lowers domestic rates and raises NCO
repairQuestions.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
repairQuestions.feedback: Lower national saving raises the domestic real rate, making domestic assets relatively attractive and reducing NCO.

bridgeQuestions.q: A deficit-funded increase in government purchases is accompanied by lower domestic investment and a real currency appreciation. A report observes these changes and claims total AD must have fallen. Which conclusion can be defended without response magnitudes?
options: Lower investment and lower NX offset part of the direct government-purchases stimulus; total AD’s direction requires their relative sizes
Real appreciation proves the NX decline exceeds the government-purchases increase
Higher government purchases prove total AD rises regardless of crowding out and NX
Lower domestic investment shifts short-run aggregate supply rather than any AD component
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Real appreciation tends to lower NX, and higher rates can crowd out investment. Both subtract from AD relative to the direct rise in G. The signs identify competing contributions, not their total. This transfers the open-economy mechanism without claiming instant or complete adjustment.

easy.q: Net exports equal which difference?
options: National saving minus consumption
Domestic investment minus national saving
Exports minus imports
Imports minus exports
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Net exports measure domestic sales abroad less domestic purchases of foreign goods and services.

easy.q: When exports exceed imports, how is the trade balance described?
options: A net capital inflow by definition
A trade surplus
A trade deficit
Balanced trade
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Exports greater than imports make net exports positive, which is a trade surplus.

easy.q: Which transaction is a U.S. export?
options: A Canadian household buys software produced by a U.S. firm
A U.S. household buys a television produced in Korea
A U.S. fund buys bonds issued by Canada
A German firm buys shares issued by a U.S. firm
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: An export is a domestically produced good or service purchased by a foreign buyer.

easy.q: In the standard open-economy accounts, which identity links trade in goods and services to trade in assets?
options: NX = C + I
NCO = G − T
S = C + NX
NX = NCO
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Net exports equal net capital outflow as an accounting identity.

easy.q: Positive net capital outflow means that domestic residents' purchases of foreign assets are:
options: Equal to domestic investment
Excluded from the international accounts
Greater than foreign purchases of domestic assets
Less than foreign purchases of domestic assets
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: NCO subtracts foreign purchases of domestic assets from domestic purchases of foreign assets.

easy.q: Why are imports subtracted in the expenditure approach to GDP?
options: Because imports are transfers rather than purchases
To remove foreign production already included in C, I, or G
Because buying imports reduces domestic production by the same amount
To treat imports as domestic intermediate goods
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Imported spending can first appear in C, I, or G, so subtracting imports prevents foreign production from being counted as domestic output.

easy.q: An exchange rate of 1.30 euros per dollar means that one dollar can buy:
options: About 0.77 euro
1.30 euros
0.30 euro
About 1.77 euros
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: The quotation states the foreign-currency amount obtainable for one dollar.

easy.q: If the dollar rises from 0.90 euro per dollar to 0.98 euro per dollar, the dollar has:
options: Appreciated against the euro
Depreciated against the euro
Kept the same value
Appreciated against every foreign currency
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: One dollar now buys more euros, so the dollar has appreciated.

easy.q: When the domestic currency depreciates, its purchasing power over foreign goods generally:
options: Rises
Remains fixed by definition
Becomes equal to domestic inflation
Falls
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A depreciated currency buys fewer units of foreign currency and therefore less foreign output, other things equal.

easy.q: Which quotation is the reciprocal of 2 dollars per pound?
options: 1.50 pounds per dollar
0.20 pound per dollar
0.50 pound per dollar
2 pounds per dollar
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Taking the reciprocal of 2 dollars per pound gives 1/2 pound per dollar.

easy.q: A stronger domestic currency means that one unit of domestic currency buys:
options: More domestic currency
More foreign currency
Less foreign currency
The same amount of every good
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Appreciation raises the foreign-currency value of each unit of domestic currency.

easy.q: A U.S. traveler benefits directly when the dollar appreciates because:
options: Each dollar buys more foreign currency
Each foreign-currency unit buys more dollars
U.S. exports become cheaper to foreign buyers
Dollar prices of all U.S. goods must fall
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A stronger dollar increases the traveler's foreign purchasing power.

easy.q: The real exchange rate compares the price of:
options: One currency with itself at two banks
Domestic goods with foreign goods after currency conversion
Domestic bonds with foreign bonds before conversion
Current domestic output with past domestic output
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: The real exchange rate converts prices into common units to compare domestic and foreign goods.

easy.q: Using e as foreign currency per domestic currency, which formula gives the real exchange rate?
options: e × domestic price level ÷ foreign price level
e × foreign price level ÷ domestic price level
Domestic price level ÷ e
Foreign price level − domestic price level
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: With this quotation, ε = eP/P*, the foreign-goods value of a domestic basket.

easy.q: Use ε = eP/P*, where e is foreign currency per domestic currency, P is the domestic price level and P* the foreign price level. A higher real exchange rate under the course convention indicates:
options: A real depreciation of the domestic currency
A lower domestic price level by definition
Purchasing-power parity must hold exactly
A real appreciation of the domestic currency
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A higher value means domestic goods are expensive relative to foreign goods, which is a real appreciation.

easy.q: Purchasing-power parity is best viewed as:
options: A rule that transportation costs are zero
A guarantee that all goods trade internationally
A long-run benchmark linking exchange rates to relative price levels
An exact daily forecast for every currency
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: PPP predicts that currency values tend to reflect relative price levels over long horizons, subject to important frictions.

easy.q: Use ε = eP/P*, where e is foreign currency per domestic currency, P is the domestic price level and P* the foreign price level. If the nominal exchange rate and foreign price level are fixed while the domestic price level rises, the domestic currency experiences:
options: A nominal depreciation
A real appreciation
A real depreciation
No real exchange-rate change
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: In ε = eP/P*, a higher domestic price level raises the real exchange rate.

easy.q: Why can PPP fail for haircuts across countries?
options: Haircuts are nontraded services with limited cross-border arbitrage
Haircuts have no prices
Exchange rates apply only to manufactured goods
PPP requires domestic inflation to be zero
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A haircut cannot easily be shipped across borders, so price gaps need not be arbitraged away.

easy.q: Net capital outflow equals domestic purchases of foreign assets minus:
options: Exports of domestic goods
Domestic investment spending
Foreign purchases of domestic assets
Domestic purchases of domestic assets
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: The second side of NCO records foreign acquisition of domestic assets.

easy.q: A U.S. resident buys a bond issued by the German government. This transaction:
options: Counts as U.S. domestic investment
Increases U.S. NCO
Decreases U.S. NCO
Increases U.S. imports
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A domestic purchase of a foreign asset is a capital outflow and enters positively in NCO.

easy.q: A Japanese pension fund buys shares in a U.S. company. For the United States, this transaction:
options: Decreases NCO
Increases NCO
Increases exports by the share price
Reduces domestic investment
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A foreign purchase of a domestic asset is subtracted when calculating domestic NCO.

easy.q: Negative NCO is also called:
options: Net capital outflow
A trade surplus
Balanced asset trade
Net capital inflow
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: When foreign purchases of domestic assets are larger, funds flow into the country on net.

easy.q: In the standard model, a higher domestic real interest rate tends to make domestic assets:
options: Identical to foreign assets
Unrelated to capital flows
More attractive relative to foreign assets
Less attractive relative to foreign assets
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A higher return draws funds toward domestic assets, other things equal.

easy.q: Political instability that causes residents to seek foreign assets is called:
options: Balanced trade
Capital flight
Crowding in
Purchasing-power parity
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Capital flight is a sharp increase in desired purchases of foreign assets prompted by risk or instability.

easy.q: In the NCO-based open-economy model, which goods-market activity creates demand for domestic currency?
options: Foreign buyers of domestic net exports
Domestic residents buying foreign assets
The domestic central bank buying domestic goods
Domestic firms purchasing domestic labor
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Foreign buyers need domestic currency to purchase domestic goods and services, creating currency demand.

easy.q: In the NCO-based model with vertical currency supply, what determines the supplied quantity?
options: Domestic consumption
Government purchases
Foreign net exports
Net capital outflow
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Residents supply domestic currency when they acquire foreign assets, so currency supply equals NCO.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what exchange rate do D0 and S0 intersect?
options: 1.2 foreign-currency units per dollar
1.5 foreign-currency units per dollar
1.0 foreign-currency unit per dollar
0.8 foreign-currency unit per dollar
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at 1.0 foreign-currency unit per U.S. dollar.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What quantity of domestic currency is exchanged at point A?
options: 160 units
100 units
80 units
120 units
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Point A projects to 100 units on the horizontal axis.

easy.q: Under a foreign-currency-per-domestic-currency quotation, an upward movement in the exchange rate represents:
options: Domestic-currency appreciation
Domestic-currency depreciation
An increase in NCO by definition
A decline in foreign prices only
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A higher foreign-currency price of one domestic-currency unit is an appreciation.

easy.q: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. If demand for domestic currency rises while supply is fixed, the equilibrium exchange rate:
options: Falls
Stays fixed
Becomes equal to NCO
Rises
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A rightward demand shift along unchanged supply raises the currency's equilibrium value.

easy.q: In the standard open-economy model, a larger government budget deficit first reduces:
options: Foreign saving
Net exports by accounting definition
The domestic price level
National saving
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: A larger deficit lowers public saving and therefore national saving when private saving is unchanged.

easy.q: A decline in national saving shifts the supply of loanable funds:
options: Vertically upward without changing quantity
Into the foreign-exchange demand curve
Left
Right
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: National saving supplies loanable funds, so less saving shifts that supply left.

easy.q: When the domestic real interest rate rises, net capital outflow tends to:
options: Equal government purchases
Fall
Rise
Remain fixed
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Higher domestic returns make domestic assets more attractive, reducing NCO.

easy.q: A fall in NCO shifts the supply of domestic currency in foreign exchange:
options: Left
Right
Down along the same vertical curve
Into currency demand
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Fewer net foreign-asset purchases mean less domestic currency is supplied for exchange.

easy.q: A real appreciation tends to change net exports in which direction?
options: Up
Toward domestic investment
Not at all
Down
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Appreciation makes domestic goods relatively expensive and foreign goods relatively cheap, reducing NX.

easy.q: Capital flight begins with an increase in desired:
options: Foreign purchases of domestic goods
Domestic tax revenue
Foreign-asset purchases
Domestic consumption only
easy.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
easy.feedback: Political or economic risk can prompt residents and investors to move portfolios toward foreign assets.

medium.q: Exports are $720 billion and imports are $810 billion. What is net exports?
options: −$1.53 trillion
$1.53 trillion
−$90 billion
$90 billion
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: NX = $720 billion − $810 billion = −$90 billion, a trade deficit.

medium.q: An economy has national saving of $640 billion and domestic investment of $500 billion. What is NCO?
options: $1.14 trillion
$140 billion
−$140 billion
$500 billion
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: From S = I + NCO, NCO = $640 billion − $500 billion = $140 billion.

medium.q: A country records NCO of −$60 billion. What must its net exports equal?
options: −$60 billion
$60 billion
An amount that cannot be inferred
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: NX and NCO are equal in the accounts, so negative NCO implies an equal trade deficit.

medium.q: Domestic residents buy $240 billion of foreign assets while foreigners buy $310 billion of domestic assets. What is NCO?
options: $70 billion
$240 billion
$550 billion
−$70 billion
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: NCO = $240 billion − $310 billion = −$70 billion, indicating net capital inflow.

medium.q: A household buys a $2,000 imported computer with no other economic change. What does GDP accounting do?
options: Investment rises by $2,000 and GDP rises by $2,000
Net exports rise by $2,000 while consumption is unchanged
Consumption rises by $2,000 and imports rise by $2,000, leaving GDP unchanged
GDP falls by $2,000 because imports are subtracted
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The purchase enters consumption, while the import subtraction removes the foreign-produced computer from domestic GDP.

medium.q: If national saving is less than domestic investment, which combination is consistent with the identities?
options: Zero NCO and a trade deficit
Negative NCO and a trade deficit
Positive NCO and a trade surplus
Positive NCO and balanced trade
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: S − I equals NCO, so S below I makes NCO negative; NX = NCO makes net exports negative as well.

medium.q: At 120 yen per dollar, how many yen can $75 purchase?
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Multiply $75 by 120 yen per dollar to obtain 9,000 yen.

medium.q: The rate changes from 1.25 Canadian dollars per U.S. dollar to 1.20. What happened to the U.S. dollar?
options: It depreciated against the Canadian dollar
It appreciated against the Canadian dollar
It appreciated by 5 percent
It remained unchanged in reciprocal terms
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: One U.S. dollar buys fewer Canadian dollars, so it depreciated.

medium.q: A hotel costs 240 euros. At 0.80 euro per dollar, what is its dollar price?
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Divide 240 euros by 0.80 euro per dollar: the hotel costs $300.

medium.q: The dollar appreciates against the peso. Holding product prices fixed in their own currencies, which buyer gains purchasing power?
options: A U.S. exporter paid only in dollars
Both buyers gain the same foreign purchasing power
A U.S. buyer purchasing Mexican goods
A Mexican buyer purchasing U.S. goods
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: A stronger dollar buys more pesos, making peso-priced goods cheaper in dollar terms.

medium.q: If 1 euro buys $1.25, approximately how many euros does $1 buy?
options: 2.25 euros
0.80 euro
1.25 euros
0.25 euro
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The reciprocal of 1.25 dollars per euro is 0.80 euro per dollar.

medium.q: The exchange rate rises from 100 to 110 pesos per dollar. By what percentage does the dollar appreciate under this quotation?
options: 10 percent
9.1 percent
11 percent
110 percent
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The dollar's value rises by 10 pesos on a base of 100, so the appreciation is 10 percent.

medium.q: A domestic basket costs 120 domestic currency units; a comparable foreign basket costs 150 foreign currency units. With e = 2 foreign currency units per domestic unit and ε = eP/P*, what is ε?
options: 1.25 foreign baskets per domestic basket
1.60 foreign baskets per domestic basket
0.625 foreign basket per domestic basket
2.50 foreign baskets per domestic basket
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Convert the domestic basket: (2 foreign/domestic currency) × (120 domestic currency/domestic basket) = 240 foreign currency/domestic basket. Divide by 150 foreign currency/foreign basket to obtain 1.60 foreign baskets per domestic basket.

medium.q: Use ε = eP/P*, where e is foreign currency per domestic currency, P is the domestic price level and P* the foreign price level. The nominal rate stays fixed, domestic prices rise 6 percent, and foreign prices rise 2 percent. Approximately what happens to the real exchange rate?
options: It appreciates about 4 percent
It depreciates about 4 percent
It appreciates 8 percent
It remains unchanged
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Faster domestic inflation raises eP/P* by roughly the inflation differential, about 4 percent.

medium.q: Domestic inflation is 3 percent and foreign inflation is 8 percent. Under relative PPP, the domestic currency should:
options: Depreciate about 5 percent nominally
Appreciate about 11 percent nominally
Remain fixed because both countries have inflation
Appreciate about 5 percent nominally
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The lower-inflation currency tends to appreciate by about the 5-percentage-point inflation differential.

medium.q: Let e be foreign currency per domestic currency and ε = eP/P*. The domestic currency depreciates nominally while domestic prices grow more slowly than foreign prices. What happens to ε?
options: It stays fixed because the two changes offset
It rises because lower domestic inflation raises P/P*
It falls because both changes cause real depreciation
Its direction is ambiguous because both nominal and real rates change
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Nominal depreciation lowers e, and slower domestic inflation lowers P/P*. Both factors lower their product ε; they reinforce rather than offset.

medium.q: A domestic basket costs 100 domestic units, a comparable foreign basket costs 250 foreign units, and the nominal rate is 2.5 foreign units per domestic unit. What does PPP imply?
options: The real exchange rate is 2.5
The baskets have the same converted price
The domestic basket is twice as expensive
The foreign basket is 2.5 times as expensive
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The domestic basket converts to 250 foreign units, matching the foreign basket; ε equals 1.

medium.q: Which friction most directly allows identical tradable goods to have different converted prices?
options: Transportation costs
The definition of nominal GDP
A balanced government budget
A vertical money-supply curve
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Shipping costs create a band within which price differences may persist without profitable arbitrage.

medium.q: Residents buy $180 billion of foreign assets, and foreigners buy $125 billion of domestic assets. What is NCO?
options: $125 billion
$305 billion
$55 billion
−$55 billion
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: NCO = $180 billion − $125 billion = $55 billion.

medium.q: Residents buy $90 billion of foreign assets while foreigners buy $140 billion of domestic assets. Which description fits?
options: NCO is zero because both sides trade assets
NCO is −$50 billion, a net capital inflow
NCO is $50 billion, a net capital outflow
NCO is $230 billion, a net capital inflow
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The difference is $90 billion − $140 billion = −$50 billion.

medium.q: Domestic real interest rates rise relative to foreign rates. What happens to NCO in the standard model?
options: NCO falls
NCO rises
NCO becomes equal to domestic investment
NCO is fixed by the trade balance alone
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Domestic assets become relatively attractive, reducing domestic purchases abroad and encouraging foreign purchases at home.

medium.q: Foreign interest rates rise while the domestic real interest rate is unchanged. What is the likely effect on domestic NCO?
options: It falls
It becomes zero
It must equal national saving
It rises
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Higher foreign returns make foreign assets more attractive to domestic investors, increasing NCO.

medium.q: A domestic firm builds a factory abroad. How is the acquisition classified for the home country?
options: An import of consumer goods
Domestic residential investment
A domestic purchase of a foreign asset
A foreign purchase of a domestic asset
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Ownership of productive capital abroad is a foreign asset held by a domestic resident.

medium.q: Foreign confidence in domestic institutions improves. Holding returns fixed, what capital-flow response is most plausible?
options: NCO remains fixed because risk cannot affect asset demand
Foreign purchases of domestic assets rise, reducing NCO
Domestic purchases of foreign assets rise, increasing NCO
Foreign purchases of domestic goods fall, raising NCO
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Lower perceived risk raises foreign demand for domestic assets, increasing the term subtracted from NCO.

The rate falls from 1.2 to 1.0 and quantity falls from 150 to 100
The rate rises from 1.0 to 1.2 while quantity stays at 100
The rate remains 1.0 while quantity rises from 100 to 150

Quantity falls from 150 to 100 and the rate rises from 0.8 to 1.0

options: Supply of domestic currency shifts left
Demand for domestic currency shifts right
Supply of domestic currency shifts right
Demand for domestic currency shifts left
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Foreign buyers require more domestic currency at each exchange rate to purchase the additional exports.

medium.q: An increase in NCO changes the foreign-exchange market by shifting:
options: Domestic-currency supply right
Domestic-currency demand right
Domestic-currency supply left
Domestic-currency demand left

medium.feedback: More net foreign-asset purchases cause residents to supply more domestic currency at every exchange rate.

At every point on S0
At the horizontal-axis intercept of D0
At the intersection of D0 and S0

medium.q: Which chain correctly begins the textbook effect of a larger budget deficit?
options: National saving rises, so the real interest rate falls
Investment demand falls, so NCO rises
Currency demand rises, so public saving rises
National saving falls, so the real interest rate rises
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Lower public saving reduces loanable-funds supply and raises the equilibrium real rate.

medium.q: A higher domestic real interest rate caused by a deficit changes the foreign-exchange market by:
options: Reducing exports and shifting currency demand left first
Increasing saving and shifting currency demand right
Reducing NCO and shifting currency supply left
Increasing NCO and shifting currency supply right

medium.feedback: The higher return attracts funds toward domestic assets, so fewer domestic-currency units are supplied to acquire foreign assets.

It appreciates from 1.0 to 1.5 foreign-currency units per dollar
It depreciates from 1.5 to 1.0 foreign-currency units per dollar
It remains fixed because NX equals NCO

medium.q: Why does a real currency appreciation tend to reduce aggregate demand, holding its other components fixed?
options: It lowers net exports, a component of aggregate demand
It lowers the domestic money supply by identity
It raises government purchases
It shifts long-run aggregate supply left
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Relatively expensive domestic goods reduce exports and encourage imports, lowering NX and AD.

medium.q: An import quota directly reduces import demand. In the standard long-run open-economy model with NCO fixed, what offsets this effect?
options: A fall in national saving that raises NCO
A currency depreciation that raises exports further
A fall in domestic investment equal to the quota
A real appreciation that reduces exports and encourages other imports
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: The quota raises demand for domestic currency, but appreciation brings NX back to the level fixed by NCO.

medium.q: Political instability triggers capital flight. What happens to currency supply in foreign exchange?
options: Currency demand shifts right
It stays fixed because capital flows use asset markets
It shifts right
It shifts left
medium.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
medium.feedback: Higher NCO means more domestic currency is offered to purchase foreign assets.

hard.q: Output is $2.4 trillion, consumption is $1.5 trillion, investment is $0.4 trillion, and government purchases are $0.6 trillion. What are NX and NCO?
options: Both are $0.1 trillion
NX is −$0.1 trillion and NCO is $0.1 trillion
NX is $0.5 trillion and NCO is −$0.1 trillion
Both are −$0.1 trillion
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: NX = Y − C − I − G = 2.4 − 1.5 − 0.4 − 0.6 = −0.1 trillion; NX = NCO.

hard.q: Private saving is $420 billion, public saving is −$80 billion, and domestic investment is $390 billion. What follows?
options: National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion
National saving is −$50 billion, so NCO and NX are −$390 billion
National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are −$50 billion
National saving is $500 billion, so NCO and NX are $110 billion
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: National saving is $420 billion − $80 billion = $340 billion. Subtracting $390 billion of investment gives NCO = NX = −$50 billion.

hard.q: A student says a trade deficit proves imports destroyed an equal amount of domestic output. Which correction is best?
options: The deficit proves national saving exceeds domestic investment
The deficit records imports above exports; it does not identify the separate response of domestic production
The claim is correct because imports are subtracted from GDP
A trade deficit means domestic consumption must be falling
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Imports are subtracted to exclude foreign production from GDP. The trade balance alone does not show how domestic output changed.

hard.q: Exports rise by $40 billion and imports rise by $65 billion while other GDP components are unchanged. How do NX and GDP change?
options: Both fall by $25 billion
Both rise by $105 billion
NX falls by $25 billion while GDP rises by $25 billion
NX rises by $25 billion while GDP is unchanged
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Net exports change by $40 billion − $65 billion = −$25 billion, so the expenditure identity lowers measured GDP by $25 billion when other components are fixed.

hard.q: A country has a $90 billion trade surplus and domestic investment of $260 billion. What national saving is consistent with the accounts?
options: $170 billion
$260 billion
$440 billion
$350 billion
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: NX = NCO = $90 billion, and S = I + NCO = $260 billion + $90 billion = $350 billion.

hard.q: Across two consistently measured periods, foreign purchases of domestic bonds rise while domestic purchases of foreign assets are unchanged. Which accounting change follows, without identifying how quickly trade adjusts?
options: NCO is unchanged, while NX falls
NCO falls, while NX must rise
NCO falls, and NX must be lower in the accounts
NCO rises, and NX must be higher
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The larger foreign-purchase flow lowers NCO. NX must match NCO in consistent period accounts; this identity alone does not establish an immediate trade response to a particular bond purchase.

hard.q: The rate moves from $1.20 per euro to $1.32 per euro. Which statement is correct?
options: The euro depreciates about 9.1 percent
The reciprocal rate also rises 10 percent
The euro appreciates 10 percent against the dollar
The dollar appreciates 10 percent against the euro
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The dollar price of one euro rises by $0.12 on a $1.20 base, so the euro appreciates 10 percent.

hard.q: The pound appreciates from $1.50 to $1.65 per pound. Approximately how much does the dollar depreciate against the pound using reciprocal rates?
options: 0.1 percent
9.1 percent
10 percent
15 percent
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The reciprocal moves from 0.6667 to about 0.6061 pound per dollar, a decline of roughly 9.1 percent.

hard.q: A U.S. machine costs $48,000. The rate changes from 0.90 to 0.80 euro per dollar, with the dollar price fixed. How does its euro price change?
options: It falls from €43,200 to €38,400
It rises from €38,400 to €43,200
It falls from €53,333 to €48,000
It remains €43,200 because the dollar price is fixed
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Multiply the dollar price by euros per dollar. Dollar depreciation lowers the euro price from 48,000×0.90 to 48,000×0.80.

hard.q: A student sees the quotation fall from 1.10 dollars per euro to 1.00 dollar per euro and says the dollar depreciated. What is the error?
options: The student is correct because every lower quotation is depreciation
The euro appreciated because its dollar price fell
No currency changed because the quotation reached one
Fewer dollars are needed per euro, so the dollar appreciated
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The dollar price of the euro fell, meaning each dollar can obtain more euros than before.

hard.q: A Canadian firm compares converting the same US$200,000 receipt at 1.35 versus 1.28 Canadian dollars per U.S. dollar. Ignoring fees, how does its Canadian-dollar revenue change?
options: It falls by C$7,000
It rises by C$27,000
It falls by C$14,000
It rises by C$14,000
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Revenue changes from C$270,000 to C$256,000, a decline of C$14,000.

hard.q: A Japanese product's yen price rises 4 percent while the yen depreciates 10 percent against the dollar. Approximately what happens to its dollar price?
options: It rises about 6 percent
It falls about 6.4 percent
It rises about 14.4 percent
It falls about 14 percent
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The dollar price changes by 1.04×0.90 − 1 = −0.064, so it falls about 6.4 percent.

hard.q: Use e in foreign currency per domestic currency and ε = eP/P*. The nominal rate rises 5 percent, domestic prices rise 4 percent, and foreign prices rise 2 percent. Approximately how does the real exchange rate change?
options: It appreciates about 3 percent
It depreciates about 7 percent
It appreciates about 7 percent
It depreciates about 1 percent
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Using growth-rate approximation, Δε ≈ 5% + 4% − 2% = 7%.

hard.q: Use ε = eP/P*, where e is foreign currency per domestic currency, P is the domestic price level and P* the foreign price level. The nominal rate is unchanged, but the domestic basket rises from 100 to 110 while the foreign basket rises from 200 to 204. What is the approximate real appreciation?
options: About 12 percent
About 7.8 percent
About 2 percent
About 5.9 percent
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The price ratio changes by 1.10/1.02 − 1 ≈ 7.8 percent.

hard.q: A currency depreciates 8 percent nominally while domestic inflation exceeds foreign inflation by 3 percentage points. What is the approximate real change?
options: A 5 percent real depreciation
An 11 percent real depreciation
A 5 percent real appreciation
An 8 percent real depreciation
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The growth approximation gives −8% + 3% = −5%, so the real exchange rate falls about 5 percent.

hard.q: A student argues that equal inflation rates guarantee an unchanged real exchange rate. What is missing?
options: Domestic prices cannot be measured
PPP rules out equal inflation
The foreign price level must equal one
The nominal exchange rate may change
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Equal inflation stabilizes the price-level ratio, but nominal exchange-rate movements can still change eP/P*.

hard.q: Why does the law of one price support PPP more strongly for wheat than for apartments?
options: Wheat prices exclude storage and transport from arbitrage decisions
Apartment rents represent identical tradable units across countries
Wheat is easier to trade and arbitrage across locations
Housing services respond more directly to exchange-rate quotations
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Cross-border arbitrage is more feasible for standardized tradable goods than for location-specific housing services.

hard.q: A U.S. instrument costs $84 and a comparable foreign instrument costs 63 crowns. The quote is 0.90 crown per dollar. With both instrument prices fixed, what quote would make their converted prices equal, and how would ε = eP/P* change?
options: 1.20 crowns per dollar; ε rises from 1.20 to 1.60
0.75 crown per dollar; ε falls from 1.20 to 1.00
0.75 crown per dollar; ε stays at 1.20
0.90 crown per dollar; ε falls from 1.20 to 1.00
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Initial ε = 0.90 × 84 / 63 = 1.20. Equality requires e × 84 dollars = 63 crowns, so e = 0.75 crown/dollar and ε = 1.00. This is a nominal and real depreciation with prices fixed.

hard.q: Domestic purchases of foreign assets rise by $70 billion, while foreign purchases of domestic assets rise by $95 billion. How does NCO change?
options: It rises by $25 billion
It rises by $165 billion
It falls by $165 billion
It falls by $25 billion
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The change in NCO is +$70 billion − $95 billion = −$25 billion.

hard.q: The domestic real interest rate rises, but political risk also rises sharply. What can be concluded about NCO?
options: NCO rises because risk determines flows independently of returns
NCO is unchanged because NX = NCO forces the channels to cancel
The direction is ambiguous because the two forces push NCO oppositely
NCO falls because interest returns determine flows independently of risk
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Higher domestic returns tend to lower NCO, while greater domestic risk tends to raise it; relative magnitudes are needed.

hard.q: A student says a capital inflow means domestic residents purchased more foreign assets. What is the correction?
options: The statement is correct whenever interest rates rise
A net inflow means foreign purchases of domestic assets exceeded domestic purchases abroad
A net inflow means both asset-purchase flows were zero
A net inflow is the same as positive NCO
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: Negative NCO is generated when the foreign acquisition of domestic assets is the larger flow.

hard.q: National saving is $520 billion, domestic investment is $610 billion, and domestic residents buy $160 billion of foreign assets. How much do foreigners buy in domestic assets?
options: $250 billion
$70 billion
$160 billion
$770 billion
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: NCO = S − I = −$90 billion. Since −90 = 160 − foreign purchases, foreign purchases are $250 billion.

hard.q: Foreign investors reduce new purchases of domestic bonds while domestic investors do not change their foreign-asset purchases. What happens to NCO?
options: It falls
It is unchanged
It becomes equal to the bond price
It rises
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: A smaller foreign purchase flow reduces the term subtracted from domestic purchases abroad, raising NCO.

hard.q: Why does a higher domestic real interest rate lower NCO rather than raise it in the standard model?
options: It makes foreign assets relatively more attractive to domestic savers
It raises outward investment by increasing the return on foreign bonds
It favors domestic assets over foreign assets for both domestic and foreign investors
It attracts foreign funds that enter positively in the definition of NCO
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: The relative-return change keeps more domestic funds at home and attracts more foreign funds.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. What appreciation is associated with the demand increase?
options: An increase of 0.5 foreign-currency unit per dollar, or 50 percent
An increase of 0.2 foreign-currency unit per dollar, or 20 percent
A decrease of 0.2 foreign-currency unit per dollar, or 16.7 percent
An increase of 0.2 foreign-currency unit per dollar, or 25 percent

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Which calculation correctly describes the move from A to B after supply shifts?

hard.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand D0 is unchanged while supply shifts right from solid S0 to dashed S1. Equilibrium moves from A at quantity 100 and rate 1.0 to B at quantity 150 and rate 0.8.
hard.foreignExchangeScenario: Increase in supply of U.S. dollars

hard.q: Refer to the conceptual graph. Which event and equilibrium response fit the displayed demand shift?
options: Higher domestic NCO; the dollar depreciates and quantity rises
Weaker foreign demand for domestic exports; the dollar depreciates and quantity falls
More domestic purchases of foreign assets; the dollar appreciates and quantity falls
Stronger foreign demand for domestic exports; the dollar appreciates and quantity rises
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: D1 lies right of D0 with S0 fixed, consistent with stronger foreign demand for domestic output and a new intersection above and right of the old one.
hard.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market showing demand shifting right from D0 to D1 with supply S0 unchanged.
hard.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Dashed demand D1 lies right of solid D0 while upward-sloping S0 is unchanged. The new intersection is above and right of the original intersection. No numerical ticks are shown.
hard.foreignExchangeScenario: Conceptual increase in demand for U.S. dollars

hard.q: Refer to the conceptual graph. Which transaction change and equilibrium response fit the displayed supply shift?
options: Fewer domestic purchases of foreign assets; the dollar appreciates and quantity falls
Greater foreign demand for domestic currency; the dollar depreciates and quantity falls
More domestic purchases of foreign assets; the dollar depreciates and quantity rises
More foreign purchases of domestic goods; the dollar appreciates and quantity rises
hard.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
hard.feedback: S1 lies right of S0 with D0 fixed, consistent with more dollars supplied to purchase foreign assets and a new intersection below and right of the old one.
hard.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market showing upward-sloping supply shifting right from S0 to S1 with demand D0 unchanged.
hard.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged.
